subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58(11)-LOSS OF JOBS IN MINING INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with great interest to the speeches that have been made on the motion of the New Democratic Party. I wish to commend that party for bringing up such an important matter. However I must say that I am surprised at how lightly the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) is taking that matter. He readily admits that there is a problem in the mining industry.
Yet, in 1974, 1975 and 1976, as he mentioned, the situation may have been better than today, but every year a gradual deterioration in the mining industry was noted. Every year some new restriction was added, there were lay-offs and suddenly in an industry like INCO in Sudbury, there is a massive loss of 3,000 to 4,000 jobs.
When the Minister of Finance argues that the bad situation now prevailing in Canada is due to outside conditions, I would say that it was brought about by the poor performance of the minister and his officials. In fact the minister, his officials and their plethora of highly paid civil servants, economists and statisticians were not able to understand the situation and prevent the problem we are facing now.
It was said in the Speech from the Throne that, and I quote once more: "... high rates of unemployment and inflation are clear signals of the inadequacy of the economic strategies appropriate to simpler times..It was in the Speech from the Throne. We are aware of that situation and what is the minister's response to the present problem in the mining industry? Absolutely nothing! He is good at laughing at others and sneering at other parties, but he is unable to make a valid suggestion. He admits that tax reductions and subsidies have been granted to mining companies and multinational corporations but-as everybody knows-instead of expanding their operations and increasing their production in Canada by investing in secondary industries they invested the money and extra profits in other countries, which means they are competing with Canadian industries and contributing to the reduction and elimination of jobs in this country.
If the government had been a little smarter in the past or if, at least, it could smarten up right now, subsidies and tax credits granted to those companies should at least be made subject to reinvestment in the manufacturing sector in Canada so that we could use the primary industry to obtain minerals, process them in this country, develop our industrial production at home and create jobs.
The minister has advised miners to look for employment elsewhere, and accept the principle of job mobility. He is even cynical enough to suggest that miners divide their working hours, reduce their wages and distribute them on the basis of four working days a week. This government has created the problem and now they say to the workers: It is up to you to solve your problem, it is up to you to work out agreements between yourselves. I would like to see the miners split their time and salary with the Minister of Finance, to see if he would accept that kind of offer. If he did, let him say so and
[Mr. Caouette (Temiscamingue).1
let him actually do it instead of merely suggesting it to them! Manpower mobility! When the emphasis is on decentralization so that people in outlying areas may have jobs. So I come back once more to the government's attitude. How come the government did not use the grants and tax cuts given to corporations to get them to create secondary industries in mining areas? Northwestern Quebec is no exception. Today Noranda Mines is not mining anymore in northwestern Quebec. They only have a smelter that depends on section Horne in Noranda and other mines throughout the country. Although that plant had to lay off people, it still has 1,000 employees or so, even though it is facing competition from foreign countries, not because of material or smelting costs, but because of transportation costs to bring the material to the smelter. There are mines in western Canada, but they find it cheaper to send the material to Japan where it is smelted, because shipping costs are lower. So Canadian material is smelted in Japan, and the government does nothing to stop that and allow our smelters to smelt our own material. The government remains idle.
Recently, I urged the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) to see to it that our mines get, not grants but special transportation rates for the material going to our smelters, so that we may save jobs in Canada. We are still waiting for an answer. In such matters, the government is in no hurry to answer. Mines were and still are forced to absorb a 21 per cent cost increase because of fringe benefits, anti-pollution expenditures that did not exist before. Smelters had to absorb extra production costs as high as to 10 per cent to invest in the environment. Those are real costs absorbed by the mines, by the smelters. The government is forcing them indirectly, to get more involved in the environment, but it gives them nothing in return except tax controls, double tax controls. It prevents them from operating on a sound basis. If there is some money to be made, the government does not hesitate. It overtaxes, it double taxes in some cases, when obviously royalties should be at the provincial rather than at the federal level. Because under the Canadian constitution, direct taxation should be at the provincial rather than at the federal level.
We know that the federal government has taken over the power of taxation, which is causing great problems to these companies today. However, when we consider these problems as a whole, is Canada short of mineral ores? Absolutely not. The Minister has just said that everything depends on foreign markets, that other countries are producing nickel, copper and gold, and that those countries are our competitors. Does the fact that other countries are producing minerals warrant dividing or reducing the workload of our people, our work potential? Definitely not. Those two things are unrelated. The simple truth is that we, as Canadians, have not been able, through our government, to develop our secondary industries to the same level as some other countries like Japan or Germany, countries which, we are all aware, were destroyed during World War II. They set up for themselves financial and economic systems which are different from our own to ensure the recovery of their economies. What are we waiting for, in
November 23, 1977

Canada to change our economic system in order to put our own economy on the road to recovery? We have the skills, we have the brains to do this. The only missing factor is always the same: the money factor, the economic factor, which is the very basis of the economy.
As I said earlier, the unemployment and inflation rates clearly demonstrate that the economic methods which were established in a less complex era have now become obsolete. What alternative does the minister suggest in the address he has just made, in his crying about the New Democratic Party and the other opposition parties, what solutions, what economic changes does he suggest? Absolutely nothing. He does not get off the beaten path. What does the government do to stimulate investment in small and medium-size business? Absolutely nothing. However, in the mini-budget we find for example that these companies are allowed to invest more money in underdeveloped countries without any restriction, and that the government intends to give them more benefits so that they can invest even more money in those other countries. 1 am in no way against investment in third world countries but I think that some areas in Canada bear much similarity to the third world.
In some areas, 15 per cent are unemployed according to statistics on unemployment. Finally, the labour force is only 60 or 61 per cent. I will give an example in the province of Quebec. In my constituency of northwest Quebec, there are 14.4 per cent of unemployed and 59.8 per cent of working people. However, when you add up both, you get 74.2 per cent of the people either working or receiving some unemployment insurance. The remaining 25.8 per cent are unemployed and are no longer entitled to unemployment insurance benefits. Why are those people who are no longer contributing to production in Canada, not mentioned?
Why are they not included? They are unemployed. This means that there are almost 40.2 per cent of unemployed in an area such as the northwest. For the whole of Canada, the figure practically reaches 40 per cent. Suggestions have been made with regard to financing but no way has been sought or found to finance any new production with new funds and not only with loans as is the case now. Taxes! The Prime Minister can answer. Who is willing to lend money without interest? The Bank of Canada can create such credits based on production, not on the activities of chartered banks, not on our neighbours, but based on the Canadian production of natural resources, on the development of our own resources. When the government understands that the Bank of Canada can issue new credits according to our new rate of production, it will be wonderful. I think most members in general admit willingly that in spite of our problems, our national production still increases yearly.
Our production has been considerably reduced in the last few years, but it still increases. In view of this increase, we could issue new credits which could be distributed to create or to help medium and small businesses and the secondary industry, which would effectively enable our primary sector to operate and to develop our resources, not to export them to other countries as is the case at the present time, but to refine
Mining Unemployment
and transform them into finished products in Canada. Afterwards, the surplus of finished products could be offered on the international market. We would have then guaranteed our workers that they will be able to work in Canada.
That is the essence of the problem, Mr. Speaker, and these are the most valid answers to the problems now facing our primary sector. But the same is true for the Americans. I was a member of a parliamentary delegation some time ago and I was told in the United States that in that country the same attitude prevailed. Our government, our marvellous Liberal government has the same attitude. I was told in the United States that it is impossible to exert too much pressure on multinationals and large companies because then they will close their doors and there will be 800,000 more unemployed. Then what shall we do? We may well say: What are we to do? Well we must find means to solve this economic problem instead of copying others, especially our American neighbours.
I heard that the Islamic Bank allowed interest-free loans to countries where it operates. But the government is not intelligent enough to realize that instead of choosing to increase its debts, it would be well advised to ask the Islamic Bank how the interest-free loan system works. This method should be used and applied in Canada, and this would solve our real problems.
We finally come to the conclusion that the government is not interested in solving that problem. The only thing it is preoccupied with in this dilemma is finding a way of taxing somebody and if the problem persists, as it does, to wash its hands off the whole thing and say to the people that it is their fault. As in the case of miners for instance, they say: Not our fault, yours; share your work week with others and that will do it.
Mr. Speaker, that sums up what I had to say in concluding I would add that in the view of the Social Credit party, rather than doing things the way they have been done for years such as in 1974, 1975, 1976 and again this year-granting tax exemptions to these multinationals-the government should hand out that money to small and middle size businesses which would know how to develop the secondary sector which would in turn stimulate production within the primary sector and thus solve the problem which is now facing the mining industry in Canada.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58(11)-LOSS OF JOBS IN MINING INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I know we are dealing today with mining industry, but since the hon. member for Temiscamingue (Mr. Caouette) opened his speech with some remarks about the manufacturing industry, I would like to answer some of them. He referred to other countries like Japan and some European countries where the manufacturing industry is doing a lot better than over here. I agree. Then he said the only thing Canada needs to achieve the same success as those other countries is a better monetary policy. I challenge him to prove to us that the monetary policy in Japan and the European countries he has referred to is in any way related to the Social Credit policy. I do not think he could. What they could teach us, and from which we could no doubt benefit, has nothing to do with monetary policy.
We could look at the suggestions he made yesterday for a monetary policy which aims at preventing the outflow of

November 23, 1977
Mining Unemployment
Canadian money without government's approval and all kind of red tape. That is not the solution and would only make the problem worse.
Those of us on this side of the House know very well that things are not going well in the economy. The mining sector is an example of one area in which things are not going very well.
One comes to the House on an opposition day ready to hear the ideas that the opposition would implement if they were in power, but when one hears about a new monetary policy of the sort which the Social Credit members described yesterday, one's reaction is, "no, thanks." That is my reaction to that. As to some of the ideas that have been put forward by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) and by the Leader of the NDP (Mr. Broadbent), I would like to turn to some of them in the limited amount of time I have. The conclusion I come to is that we are better off not taking the advice that they have put forward.
Some have suggested, in their questions and comments in the House in the days past, that we could keep the miners working at their present level in Sudbury at INCO if we were prepared to begin stockpiling. Maybe it was done in the past in some other sectors, so they say, "Let us do it in this sector." I do not see that as any kind of solution to the problems that INCO is facing right now. On the contrary, as the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) indicated, that is the kind of approach that you can run with for just several months. There is $1 billion worth of nickel lying on the ground already, taken out by INCO. That is no solution because there is a limit to what the present weak Canadian economy can put in to support one particular sector.
The idea they put forward that somehow or other the developments in which Canadians are involved offshore are responsible for the problems we face at INCO has no connection. The solution does not lie in continuing forced production in a world which temporarily does not have any demand for the amount of nickel which can be produced.
The solution lies in ideas like the one suggested by the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Cullen), job sharing. On the subject of job sharing I want to extend that concept a little further than it has been extended in this House so far. Job sharing is not relevant just to workers who have been laid off from a particular industry. I suggest that we ought to be looking into job sharing for the benefit of young people who are coming into the labour force and finding- temporarily, I again insist-that they cannot get good well paying jobs because the labour force, growing at a rate of over 200,000 new jobs a year, is just not growing fast enough to take them in. They have a claim to job sharing in the same way workers who are being laid off have a claim to job sharing.
I would like to see a little less respect from the NDP for the vested interests which exist for existing jobs, and a little more willingness to explore the kinds of solutions which a regrettably slow growing economy has to face. We must face up to

the kinds of solutions which will provide employment for young people in tough times and which will make it easier for people who are about to be laid off. Stockpiling certainly is not the solution.
Hon. members of the NDP indicate that the Canadian government should not have helped Canadian companies like INCO to find business opportunities offshore. Taking that further, they say we ought to remove incentives and that we ought in fact to have positive disincentives in order to force Canadian industry to remain in Canada and not to go looking offshore.
Let us first look at our motivation for going offshore. We are going offshore partly because that is a responsibility developed countries have to developing countries. Developed countries must assist developing countries to realize their potential. We are also going offshore to find jobs for Canadian workers and to find profits for Canadian companies. Canada benefits when Canadian enterprises find offshore opportunities.
I visited a nickel project in Guatemala. I went through the plant and met the workers there. I saw a lot of Canadian equipment in that operation. If that Guatemalan project had been developed by some other country-as it inevitably would have been because it is a very good project-we would not see Canadian engineers working there and we would not see Canadian equipment going to the project to the extent we do. When Canadian companies go offshore, Canada benefits. The companies get extra profits, there is more manufacturing output for Canadian enterprises, and extra jobs are created for Canadian engineers who direct, organize, and get these projects off the ground. That is all to the good.
There was also some objection to foreign ownership. INCO is not a case of that, but it was argued that we ought to do more to promote Canadian ownership in the mining sector. I want to say a word about that because I am very strongly in favour of Canadian ownership. As much as anyone I recognize the dangers of heavy foreign ownership of certain sectors of the Canadian economy; for example, in manufacturing where there is a truncation and a fragmentation which take place because of the extent of foreign ownership. However, I would like to make it very clear that, in my opinion, foreign ownership is not a negative feature when it comes to mining. The mines are here in Canada. The identity of their owners and their nationality are very much less important than in any other sector.
I would go so far as to say that as much as Guatemala is prepared to welcome Canadian investors who want to come and see opportunities developed for the benefit of both sides, Canada should be prepared and should continue to be prepared to welcome foreign investors who want to come and support Canadian mining opportunities and see them developed. I do not think there is any negative side to it. I do not think Canada loses anything when the development of our mines takes place through foreign owners. It is not that we should not encourage Canadian ownership in the mining field. I do not want to take the time to describe the tax benefits and
November 23, 1977

the allowances which are available to encourage Canadians, and which are not available to foreigners. We do what we can, but I do not think we should be worried about the extent of foreign ownership in the mining sector.
I want, in the remaining time at my disposal, to talk about taxation issues. The NDP made a great deal of the amount of incentive and encouragement the tax system has given to mining in Canada. When the Conservatives speak, they will no doubt emphasize the other side of it, the enormous burden- referred to by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain-we place on the mining sector which prevents it from doing the kind of job it wants to do and which our resources justify.
On the one hand, the NDP says we have imposed too little taxation, and on the other hand, the Conservatives say that taxation has been a very serious burden for the mining industry. I want to suggest-and refer to some statistics-that the level of taxes imposed by the federal government is very much in line with the taxation other countries impose on their mining sectors. After all, that is the important thing. Investment in mining is very mobile. It is ready to go to countries which are ready to encourage it to come to them. I think it is extremely important for us to have a taxation system in the mining field which is comparable to the taxation systems which exist in other countries. I want to suggest that we do have that kind of system.
Let me refer to some evidence which was put before the Senate banking committee by the president of Noranda. He came to the Senate to complain about the very high level of taxation in the mining industry. As far as the federal government is concerned, I think he was laying a bum rap on us. He used the example of Brenda Mines in British Columbia. He hypothetically translated its activities for the year 1975-I believe it was-into what would have happened in Ontario and Nevada if that exact mining operation had been conducted in those places. He found that the over-all burden of taxation on profits was discouraging and, as he said, devastating, in Canada. I agree with him. I think the over-all aggregate level of taxation in Canada on the mining sector is very much too high, and I think that explains why new mines have been opening at a very slow rate in the last few years.
The actual tax burden Brenda paid that year in British Columbia was 71 per cent of its profit. If the Brenda mining operation for that year had been conducted in Ontario the burden of taxation would have been 49 per cent, while in Nevada the rate would have been 28 per cent. So to repeat, to keep the figures before the House, in British Columbia it was 71 per cent in that year; in Ontario, it would have been 49 per cent; and in Nevada, it would have been only 28 per cent.
Then the president of Noranda Mines did a further calculation. He indicated what the difference would have been if the prices of the product sold by the mine had doubled, costs unchanged, but prices doubled. He showed the results would have been worse. In British Columbia, instead of paying 71 per
Mining Unemployment
cent in taxes the company would have had to pay 83 per cent. In Ontario, instead of paying 49 per cent it would be 56 per cent, and in Nevada, the company, instead of paying 28 per cent, it would be 31 per cent. The president of Noranda called this burden incredibly perverse. It is obvious, with tax levels of 83 per cent, you would not have any new mines encouraged or any mining encouraged at all.
I might note that the burden of taxation in British Columbia was introduced by the NDP government which was defeated subsequently. To the extent it is still in the province, it is a legacy, an NDP policy.
Here we have the NDP saying we need a new industrial mining policy.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58(11)-LOSS OF JOBS IN MINING INDUSTRY
speechtext: That is true.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58(11)-LOSS OF JOBS IN MINING INDUSTRY
speechtext:
I am glad they were not more specific about what the policy would have been, because if they had recommended the policy their colleagues in British Columbia actually introduced, with companies having to pay a rate of tax of 71 per cent, and as high as 83 per cent in the hypothetical case introduced by Noranda, you can imagine what kind of mining operations we would have in this country.
A point the president of Noranda Mines did not emphasize in his testimony was a comparison of where the taxes were being paid, what proportion was going to the federal government, and what proportion was going to provincial governments. He presented several charts with his evidence, but he did not refer to them very specifically in giving his testimony. The charts showed Canadian federal tax compared to American federal tax was within 10 per cent. There was only a 10 per cent difference between Canadian tax and the American federal tax on the Brenda Mines' operations of that year. Although the aggregate burden was 71 per cent in Canada versus 28 per cent in the United States, nearly triple the total, the Canadian tax was within 10 per cent. In the operation of the higher profits example he gave, Canadian federal taxation would actually have been lower than in the United States.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58(11)-LOSS OF JOBS IN MINING INDUSTRY
speechtext: How come you are not specific in these numbers?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58(11)-LOSS OF JOBS IN MINING INDUSTRY
speechtext:
The hon. member has asked for specific numbers. I could table the charts if the House would allow me to do so. The Canadian federal tax is not particularly out of line. As I have indicated in the higher price example, it is lower. In the B.C. higher profit case, if Ottawa took no tax at all the burden on the company would still have seen more than double in British Columbia than in Nevada. In other words, Canada's federal tax on mining-and this is a conclusion from these figures-is no worse, and it is usually more favourable than tax in the United States.
The mining companies of Canada when they come to Parliament complain tremendously about their tax burden. They are entitled to complain because the burden is too high but it is not a matter that the federal government can cure. In the case of new oil prices, a company, with profits, which does maximum

November 23, 1977
Mining Unemployment
exploration here in Canada, can reduce its federal tax rate to 4 per cent of its total taxable income.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58(11)-LOSS OF JOBS IN MINING INDUSTRY
speechtext: Nonsense. Where do you manufacture those prices?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58(11)-LOSS OF JOBS IN MINING INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Federal taxes on oil can be reduced to 4 per cent. On hard rock, as I have indicated, they are well within line of the level of taxation in the United States.
Members opposite, particularly the hon. member for Qu'Ap-pelle-Moose Mountain, made a case out of the fact that the royalty deductibility was disallowed by the federal government. That sounds fairly serious. It did increase the tax burden they pay to the provinces. What has to be borne in mind is that natural resources are primarily provincial assets. The provinces are entitled to royalties from these assets. They are also national resources, and the federal taxpayers, as a whole, are as entitled to draw some federal revenue from those enterprises as they are from any other businesses that are conducted in this country.
Take the example of the province of Alberta, and the members opposite from Alberta can stand up to try to defend the Alberta government on this point. It tried to cut out the share to which the federal taxpayer is entitled from oil revenues. That just could not be accepted by the federal government representing federal taxpayers as a whole.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58(11)-LOSS OF JOBS IN MINING INDUSTRY
speechtext: We do not know what you are talking about.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58(11)-LOSS OF JOBS IN MINING INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Hon. members say I do not know what I am talking about, but they can stand up when their turn comes and try to make their case.
I think there is a lot to be done to encourage the mining industry, particularly the hard rock mining industry. But, it is a bum rap to try to argue that the federal government has a disincentive tax policy, Mr. Speaker, because it does not.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58(11)-LOSS OF JOBS IN MINING INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am going to make some remarks on this motion which is very good indeed and which is further reinforced by the amendment put forward by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton). I think it completes a motion which highlights a tremendously interesting subject, given the situation in which we are now.
Of course I read carefully the motion which:
... condemns the lack of action by the federal government to prevent the serious loss of jobs in Canada's mineral industry ...
To be less severe, I would not say that the government did absolutely nothing but that what it did is far from being sufficient, and this was proved, I think. We on this side believe it would be a very good idea to call in the provinces and to cooperate with them, leaving them of course some responsibility in the establishment of the priorities which could be coordinated by the efforts of a federal government, through the

establishment of an industrial strategy, of a long term policy which could only improve the situation.
I also listened carefully to the hon. member for York Centre (Mr. Kaplan) who seems, as a matter of habit, to accept the situation. Making a series of comparisons he explained that in view of the efforts of the federal government, we should be satisfied with the present situation. Besides, by mentioning the reduction of the work week to four days, I feel that he has just given proof of his government's inability to get us out of the doldrums, as far as the mining industry is concerned. In fact I think that if we agree in principle that we should ask the labour unions and the workers for work sharing status, it automatically proves that the federal government is really determined to maintain the million of unemployed which we have now in this country.
To such comments, we say: No! An unequivocal no, and we believe that this government has failed in this area, as well as in many others. We share the government's desire to help other countries, but we believe that the Canadian worker and the Canadian industry are entitled to a reasonable degree of protection. We also share this idea of giving Canadians a chance to work abroad, to be better known outside Canada but that some leading Canadians ought not to be forced to go into exile to work, which is exactly what is happening at this time.
Under the present circumstances, I repeat that this motion is very timely and that it brings about our deep concern about the layoffs taking place in the mining sector. The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner) and the Minister of Finance have suggested that there could be more. We know perfectly well that in the province of Quebec and in other provinces, we must expect other layoffs which, once more, will increase the unemployment rate. Personally, I believe that there has been a failure which we, on this side of the House condemn: a lack of communication between the federal government and the business community, the employers, the workers and the provinces. In our system, there is no way out unless we can rely upon the collaboration and the understanding from business, labour and the provincial governments. I think this is the solution for a government which will decide to be more open and responsible in those very important fields of our economy in order to solve the present problems we are facing in the mining industry. But this lack of consultation and communication is the direct consequence of the situation which is now prevailing. We are concerned that our low productivity and our high wages may reduce our competitive power and leave us trailing behind other countries. What has this government done to make both industry and labour aware of the dangers which may occur if we do not reach a good level of communication and sincere co-operation in the most important fields, with regard to our long-term policies.
In the remarks he made earlier, the Minister of Finance recognized that we were in a very difficult situation, which seemed to surprise him. He tried to bring us to his viewpoint
November 23, 1977

by telling us: "We are prepared to do something but, after all, a whole series of events took place and brought about this situation." And we, of course, in a spirit of fair play, could perhaps say to the Minister of Finance: we hold you to your word and we will forget the past, the faults, the failure, the weaknesses of your policies and particularly the lack of those, and we will start thinking as you do, that better days are ahead. I think that we should regret, deplore and condemn the government for this lack of market studies, for this failure to work together as I mentioned a while ago, and to co-operate with representatives of all sectors of the economy who could help the government bring about a recovery. A government that would be thinking otherwise certainly could not get the confidence of the members of this side of the House. It is impossible to have any confidence in this government, because of its regrettable attitude which is responsible for the situation we are experiencing now.
Somebody spoke about the drain of capital, there again, it would have been necessary to bring around to the same table investors and managers and explain to them the importance of reinvesting a percentage of their profits in a secondary or a processing industry. Once again there is a lack of contact with the business community, Mr. Speaker, and we easily realize the reluctance of the businessman today. He is waiting to see what will be the long-term policy of the government. The Minister of Finance replied to a question of mine concerning the advisability of holding a meeting of the Ministers of Finance more especially from the Maritimes and Quebec: "Well, I am always ready to welcome them." I feel that the government was wrong not to grant funds for research. As I said a few days ago, Senator Lamontagne recently blamed his government for failing to allot sufficient funds for research. Of course, some are always asking for further expenditures, but the lack of research is, in my opinion, responsible for the conditions which we are now experiencing.
I think that this lack of adequate funds has kept the government from drafting and presenting a long term policy. This lack of adequate funds has also prevented the government from urging certain basic or traditional industries in the mining sector and in others to modernize and improve the Canadian industry and to foresee the relevant markets and changes. This lack of research has also stopped the creation of new products which were increasingly required; research and new product designs were left to a neighbouring country and we were content to play second fiddle.
Again, this lack of research has made Canadians and businessmen unsure of the stability of our Canadian industry. The government is to be blamed for failing to come up with a prevention policy. Ministers one after the other since the opening of this session admit that we are in a difficult situation, they regret and deplore the present situation, they are seeking our confidence and they are asking us to regain public confidence, but this lack of prevention must be very severely

condemned, Mr. Speaker, and I think we must remind the government that it is impossible to renew this confidence, which the government requests despite this incredible shortcoming, through a lack of foresight when it is very well known that to govern is to see ahead, Mr. Speaker. In these circumstances, the government has been seen making incredible efforts in the application of social legislation.
Everyone knows and all Canadians know that the government, through its public servants and experts, has been satisfied to invent social legislation to try to compensate for the lack of courageous or positive policies and initiatives for our Canadian industries. This is where this government has brought us, Mr. Speaker. I recently asked the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie) to call a meeting with his provincial counterparts as soon as possible. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) told us that this meeting would probably take place within four days. ment helps those sectors facing problems. Some sectors, Mr. Speaker, as everybody knows, face problems, particularly in the field of transportation or in areas remote from the large centres. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, contrary to what the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle) has just said, I will refrain from rhetoric and stick to the point. Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to join in this debate on the problems INCO mining is facing in Sudbury and Thompson. To start with, I would like to remind the House that the Minister of Employment and Immigration and his senior officials lost no time in making specific federal services and programs constantly available to the workers and the industry.
As soon as INCO corporation's difficulties were known, senior officials from the Employment and Immigration Commission attended a meeting in Toronto, on October 25 which was also attended by INCO management and union representatives to study the question of the impending lay-offs announced by INCO. That company had announced that it intended to lay off some 2,800 workers in Sudbury, Ontario and 650 others in Thompson, Manitoba. Later, on October 31, officials from the Employment and Immigration Commission of Canada met with representatives from that corporation and from the labour union in Winnipeg to conduct a specific study of the situation in Thompson. Officials from the Ontario government attended the Toronto meeting while officials from the Manitoba government attended the Winnipeg meeting.
The purpose of those meetings was two-fold. First it aimed at ascertaining whether those forthcoming lay-offs were of a temporary or permanent nature. The second was to find the best ways for the Canadian government and the Canada Employment and Immigration Commission in particular to help solve the problems arising out of the proposed lay-offs. The commission officers therefore outlined the various programs and services that could be used by the workers involved, which I will now review. In the first place we have employment services, and in this case special arrangements are made to increase the normal services, in order that offices in the communities faced with lay-offs are made aware of the jobs available in various mines throughout the country. More specifically, the manpower consultative service closely cooperates with industry to give as fast and efficient service as possible.
In cases where lay-offs are notified, special committees have been or can be set up through the MCS to launch joint employer-employee efforts to determine the most adequate
November 23, 1977

solutions to the unemployment problem. In particular, this could determine the most appropriate ways to use and coordinate programs and other forms of department help to solve the current problems. In July 1977, Employment and Immigration Canada thusly found jobs for 1,400 miners.
Let us now turn, Mr. Speaker, to mobility grants. They can be given to jobless workers who need help to locate where employment opportunities exist. The mining industry has benefitted to a significant degree from the manpower mobility program. Some 34 per cent of workers who relocated under the program in 1974-75 found jobs in other mines. Only 4.4 per cent left mining, a significant gain to the mining industry.
We have also offered our training programs. They can be dispensed to unemployed miners wishing to acquire new skills in related or different jobs. In 1974-75, $2,100,000 or 5.7 per cent of the total help under the Manpower Canada industrial training program were granted to mines, quarries and oil well workers.
As the Minister of Employment and Immigration pointed out from the outset of his representations, we will also have our direct job creation programs. The usual type of projects provided by Canada Works could not be the best form of help for the highly skilled mine workers but could undoubtedly provide employment for certain less skilled workers. A much more substantial and important contribution could come from the job creation projects available to other people in the community whose incomes and stability of employment would be adversely affected by the reduced activity of the mining industry itself.
There is also unemployment insurance, Mr. Speaker, which is obviously the most direct and immediate way of dealing with the problem of the income of the unemployed. Nor should it be forgotten that the latest statistics for the second quarter of 1977 show that about 9,000 claimants had previously been employed in mines or related operations. During the meetings held in Toronto and Winnipeg, the management of INCO indicated its intention of co-operating fully in the help that could be provided so the relocated workers could find other jobs. As a matter of fact, since those meetings took place management representatives and labour union leaders continued their collective bargaining and employment and immigration senior officials were kept informed of the proceedings. For example, management made an inventory of available workers and their skills. It helped identify other businesses which would be interested in recruiting INCO workers. Similarly, it arranged interviews for that purpose and gave time off to the workers involved. Talks were also held to make training programs available to INCO workers which could use them to find new jobs.
In addition, Mr. Speaker, the INCO management and the union representatives have studied the possibility of cutting down the number of lay-offs through early retirement. As everybody knows, Mr. Speaker, the Canada Employment and Immigration Commission has introduced a new work-sharing program but the company and the union did not see fit to carry discussions any further, at least for the time being.

The Canada Employment and Immigration Commission is following up the situation at INCO, which includes conversations between company and union representatives and the action of the Ontario government. In fact, the Ontario legislature created a special committee to study the situation and report on actions to be taken to offset the numerous lay-offs which are contemplated by INCO. One can see, Mr. Speaker, that the federal government has been involved in a common effort with company, union and provincial government spokesmen to settle as quickly and as efficiently as possible all problems regarding the lay-offs considered by INCO. I must say that had the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle) been ready to help the government, he should have taken this opportunity to be more positive.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in participating in this debate I first of all listened to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) outline the only solution which the government has come up with in regard to the lay-offs specifically in the mining industry and indeed in the entire resource sector. This proposal was reiterated by the hon. member for York Centre (Mr. Kaplan). The proposal involved work-sharing.
It is very obvious, Mr. Speaker, that the ministers of this government do not even talk to each other, and needless to say their parliamentary secretaries are treated just like the back benchers on the government side of the House. They very well know that the proposal regarding work-sharing was immediately tossed out when it was proposed by the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) to INCO and Falconbridge. It was suggested that work-sharing be adopted by INCO and Falconbridge in connection with the lay-offs at Sudbury, Port Colborne, and at Thompson, but the whole concept of work sharing was thrown out. In effect, INCO and Falconbridge told the minister in no uncertain terms that these lay-offs are going to go beyond one year and that they do not know beyond one year whether the men would ever be recalled.
The hon. member for York Centre also talked about worksharing as being the coming solution to our unemployment problem. I am waiting for the hon. member for York Centre to start sharing his job with an unemployed miner. Perhaps if we had enough unemployed miners sharing the jobs of Liberal members we would get some mineral policies in this country.
I had a very remarkable morning, Mr. Speaker. First of all I spoke to the Canadian Paperworkers Union's annual convention in the city of Toronto. Many members were there as delegates to that convention from the province of Quebec, Atlantic Canada, the west coast, and the province of Ontario. After speaking to that convention I had another meeting this morning which was rather significant. I had a meeting with the president of Falconbridge Nickel Mines, Mr. Marsh Cooper, with respect to the particular situation in the Sudbury basin vis-a-vis the employees at the Falconbridge operation.

November 23, 1977
Mining Unemployment
As I flew back to Ottawa this afternoon, Mr. Speaker, I thought about the resource industry of Canada, and what came to my mind immediately was a speech, which I thought I had seen somewhere before, by a Mr. Henry S. Wingate, who had been the Chairman of the Board of the International Nickel Company of Canada. He made a speech on February 18, 1971, and I should like to read a part of the speech to the House because I think it is very significant. If I may quote him, he said:
"The unusual capacity of the mining industry to create wealth for an economy, to literally turn what was once rock or dirt into a valuable metal, and in the process to generate jobs and a large number of supporting industries, needs to be more fully understood by the public generally and by government officials".
In other words, God created INCO and INCO created the nickel in Sudbury and Thompson.
Before I went north to the Nickel Belt in 1962,1 was part of the great mass of the Canadian people who had always taken the resources of Canada for granted. I did not appreciate the implications of those resources, and in particular the nonrenewable resources. It was only after living in the Nickel Belt for some time and seeing the miners at work and listening to them that I understood the nature of the mining industry.
Living in the Sudbury Basin almost at the confluence of two major railroads going east-west and north-south, we are always aware of the north-south traffic. We see the ore cars taking out iron ore, nickel and copper pellets on their journey south, and this same railway system bringing back into the north finished products to be sold to the residents of the northern communities. Those thoughts were with me as I contemplated our non-renewable resources.
One of the things we must keep in mind is that extracting resources from the ground is a very capital intensive operation. That was the first conclusion I came to after seeing it in operation in the Nickel Belt. Indeed, on checking with Statistics Canada I discovered that to create one job in the extractive process, in other words taking the ore out of the ground, it costs $200,000. It cost that much just to put one job in the extractive process into place.
On the other hand, to create one job in the manufacturing, secondary sector of the mining industry it costs $40,000. We immediately come to the conclusion, therefore, that when those resources are taken out, and I have said this in the House many times in the past, these resources are the key to unlocking other sources of wealth for not only this generation of Canadians, but for future generations.
In other words, if we are to get the benefit of these nonrenewable resources we must take the capital generated from the sale of them and ensure that it is invested in establishing an infrastructure which will put into place secondary manufacturing industries related to the primary. I have asked myself, is that being done in the Sudbury Basin?
I was born and raised in a Third World country and saw Alcan exploit the bauxite resources of Guyana. Alcan then put the bauxite on ships and brought it to Arvida on the St.

Lawrence where it was manufactured into aluminum. I lived with that, but I have come to one of the most progressive countries in the world, and I am very proud to be part of it, and lo and behold I find that in 1977, and this has been going on for nigh on 50 years, Falconbridge Nickel still ships out the nickel matte-that is the product after semi-processing-to Norway where the company has its refinery, and it is there refined into a finished product and presumably sold back to Canada.
I do not understand how a progressive government with any sort of policy in respect of the non-renewable mineral sector of this country would ever have permitted that situation to exist for so long. Indeed, it was surprising to hear the Minister of Finance say to my leader, the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent), a few minutes ago that he agreed with us that we needed an industrial strategy. I would ask who has formed the government for the last 18 years? Indeed, which party has been the government for the last 40 years, or for the greater part of the last 50 years? I suggest it has been of the same political stripe as those sitting in those seats now.
How much longer must we wait for a strategy that makes the maximum use of the non-renewable resource sector? Indeed, the way those resources are being depleted it is shameful, an absolutely crying shame, to see INCO and Falconbridge at this point in time high-grading the ore, and that means taking out the highest quality ores now at the lowest labour cost because they bring the highest price. It is shameful on the part of this government that permits multi national corporations to rape us and carry on as though they had no responsibility whatsoever for the interests not only of this generation of Canadians but of future generations.
I can understand the reluctance of the Liberals and Conservatives to tackle the multinational mining corporations or to take them to task. I can understand how they can become the apologists, Mr. Speaker. The answer is very clear to anyone who has the time to dig out and read the information. This comes when we see the report of the Chief Electoral Officer of Canada. We find, for example, that the International Nickel Company of Canada Limited donated in the last year $30,885, to be exact, to the Conservative Party of Canada. Noranda Mines gave the Liberals and the Conservatives equally-they back both horses in the race-$16,000 each. Algoma Steel and Denison Mines gave $15,000 to each of those parties. When we look at the entire resource sector we find that every major company has rewarded the two old line parties.

-mineral policy must maintain its general goal of obtaining the best benefits for Canadians from minerals.
My question would be, has the government set out the goals very clearly and are they known to the multinational mining companies? This brings me to my interview this morning with Mr. Marsh Cooper. One of my first questions was whether the government had approached Falconbridge in order to sit down and discuss what Falconbridge's plans are from here on in with respect to the nickel and copper industries in the Sudbury Basin? Mr. Cooper's answer was, "Not at all; not at all". There has been no communication between the senior level of government in this country and the Falconbridge Nickel Mines that could determine the future lives of so many of our people.
Furthermore, in discussing the matter with Mr. Cooper, he said exactly what the apologists for the mining companies have said, and what was said by the hon. member for York Centre, the Minister of Finance, and the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner), that if INCO did not go into Indonesia and Guatemala some other company would. Well, I have to put a question to the government. Maybe these are very good goals for INCO and Falconbridge. Market dominance in lateritic nickel ores is an excellent goal for the private sector, but I would ask what are the goals of Canada in respect of its mineral resources? Are INCO's Falconbridge's goals the goals for Canadians? Is what is good enough for INCO and Falconbridge good enough for us?
It should be pointed out that 1974 was a good year for INCO. Its net profit was $300 million. One would assume and expect that the Company recognizes the need for investment and diversification of industry in Canada, and would plough back the bulk of those profits into Canadian development. What did INCO do with $242 million of that profit? It bought a battery company, ESB. As a result of that INCO is before the courts in the United States for infringing the monopoly legislation there. That is a perfect example of money earned in Canada being used to diversify the company's base by buying out a company which already exists, and not investing that money in Canada in a new industry which would create employment.
I raised the following point with Mr. Cooper today: it has been indicated that Falconbridge is doing so poorly on the stock market and in the sale of nickel that it has to lay off

workers in the Sudbury Basin, and yet Falconbridge Mines, McIntyre Mines, its parent company; Superior Oil of Texas, its grandparent company, along with Noranda Mines, have signed an agreement with the government of Chile to invest $1 billion over the next five years in the strip mining of copper in northern Chile. How does that help Canadian unemployment at this time when that investment is needed here so badly? We are saying that foreign investment should come into Canada, and yet we have Canadian investors using moneys earned from Canadian resources to invest in the southern United States, Chile, and all over the world.
In St. Lawrence, Newfoundland, Alcan has closed down an entire community. It was not because its fluorspar mine was not making profit, rather it was not making enough profit. They closed that mine down and intend to go to Mexico where they will purchase fluorspar from Noranda Mines which has a fluorspar mine there. Canadians are fed up with being used as a pawn in an international chess game which the multinational corporations play.

Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent) for putting the matter of the implementation of an effective mineral resource industrial strategy before the House for the purpose of having a day long debate.
Before getting into what I have to say, I should like to comment on one or two of the points made by the hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez). He is always a very provocative speaker, and for this reason one is tempted to react to some of the things he says. I do not want to argue for or against the concept of multinationals. However, he might well bear in mind the number of jobs that have been provided for Canadians over decades now as a result of capital that has been brought into this country, and as a result of developments that have been made in Canada by companies that perhaps have not been owned 100 per cent by Canadians, indeed where the majority of the ownership may have been outside the country. It may not be the best way for us to be doing business, but I think we must bear in mind that many Canadians today owe their livelihood to the fact that the multinationals have been here and have been established.
Whenever the hon. member for Nickel Belt quotes these large figures relating to the profits of multinational corporations, as do his colleagues in the NDP, he always refrains from

November 23, 1977
Mining Unemployment
talking about the returns on investment. Three hundred million dollars may be a great deal of money, but he does not tell us what percent of the capital it represents. Is the $300 million a 10 per cent, a 20 per cent or more profit on the money invested? These are the things that must be brought into play when one talks about profits, whether they are excessive or too little. The sum means nothing until you know what kind of money has been invested by the company in question.

speechtext:
I was not the one to raise the point. I was merely saying members opposite have a responsibility, when they are talking about excessive profits, to relate the figures they quote to the capital that has been invested in the first place.
During the two year period when I was chairman of the Standing Committee on National Resources and Public Works I found it regrettable that we were never able to undertake in the committee any kind of study of the mineral resource base in this country. I think it is the responsibility of that committee to get into this area at some point. The reason we were not able to do this is that we were preoccupied with matters relating to energy, and I am afraid the committee might continue to be preoccupied with these matters in the coming year. It has been pointed out by a number of Canadians interested in the activities of our committee that indeed we should be looking at matters relating to our mines and national resources other than those more typically associated directly wth the energy picture.
Again I welcome the opportunity of this debate on this subject and I hope we can find a mechanism in our parliamentary system to have far more discussion in this area since it is so fundamental to our over-all Canadian industrial strategy. This is a very complex issue and the implementation of a mineral resource industrial strategy for Canada involves not only the jurisdiction of the provinces over their mineral resources, as provided under the BNA Act, but also the federal government's jurisdiction in a number of joint federal and provincial areas.
The government recognizes that the Canadian minerals industry is indeed a strong and very basic industry, and it appreciates its responsibility in international trade as a secure and stable supplier of metals and minerals. The federal government, in acting in particular through the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources in co-operation with other departments, such as the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, the Department of Finance, the Department of External Affairs and, to some extent, the office of Federal-Provincial Relations, has been carrying out a great many studies in this area.
In addition to direct consultation with Canadian mining companies, the government's actions have involved numerous contacts with the provincial governments, the Mining Association of Canada, and the National Advisory Committee on the Mining Industry. At present there is an interdepartmental committee headed by the Department of Energy, Mines and

Resources, which has formed a task force with the Mining Association of Canada to study the problems of the mining industry in Canada and to make recommendations thereon.
Mineral development in Canada and throughout the world depends ultimately on market considerations. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) amplified on that this afternoon when he was discussing problems with relation to nickel and in particular, expectations respecting future market trends.
The cyclical nature of supply and demand in the international market place plays a very important part in the decisionmaking process as to whether to develop various ore deposits and the commitment of required investments into such developments. Similarly, the rate of consumption must determine the rate of production in any given market condition, and the situation today in many mineral commodities is indeed-as we are finding with regard to nickel-one of over-supply, with massive inventories overhanging world markets. This condition is further complicated by the continuation of high production rates by some developing countries which rely heavily on their exports of metals and minerals for foreign exchange earnings.

Until recently production in Canada has been maintained at fairly high levels in order to maintain employment in the communities which depend on it, and again I admit to the hon. member for Nickel Belt that the problem in Sudbury is serious, but he knows, as we all do, that 85 per cent of the work force up there is still very gainfully employed in the INCO project. I think it is important to look positively on what is going on, but we are at the same time concerned about the problems of those who are about to be laid off.
In the light of foreseeable consumption trends it has now become necessary to adjust production levels in line with the lower level of demand and to accomplish an orderly reduction of inventory. This has had a very hard impact on employment, not only in Canada but also in most countries which have been forced to take similar action. Some examples are Australia, the United States, and various countries in Europe.
The federal government has developed a number of trade policies which hopefully are benefiting the minerals industry. In this regard the government has directed that Canada participate with other interested countries, including producers and consumers, in an examination of the problems associated with commodities such as minerals, with a view to elaboration of appropriate mechanisms to stabilize markets. For this reason Canada has become a key participant in a number of forums such as the UNCTAD, the International Lead-Zinc Study Group, the Law of the Sea Conference, and the OECD, where the present and future health of the mineral industry will be advanced.
The federal government announced its policy on the further processing of resources prior to export, including mineral resources, in 1973. The objective of the policy is to process surplus natural resources prior to export wherever processing

would be internationally competitive and compatible with the development of a sound industrial structure. This policy is still being actively pursued in consultations with the provinces and with industry through federal policies respecting trade and industrial development.
The foreign investment review process and regional economic expansion are two other areas where these consultations are going on, and there is active involvement in endeavouring to maintain and develop a sound industrial structure. Where processing is hindered by measures such as tariff and nontariff measures of foreign countries which discriminate against Canadian further processed resource exports, we are seeking to negotiate substantial reductions or elimination of the effects of such measures, in both multilateral negotiations and in other appropriate ways.
The Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce has always recognized the tremendous importance of the metals and minerals sector to Canada's prosperity and export earnings, and has encouraged aggressive market activities on the part of Canadian producers and exporters, both by the mounting of trade missions to major marketing areas and through the services of the trade commissioners in posts around the world.
Recognizing that the present depressed state of world markets for most metallic mineral products will bring about further reductions in production levels, the government has made arrangements for the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources and the federal-provincial relations office to initiate discussions with the provinces where, after all, control over mineral resources still remains in so many ways. The government is also concerned with the development of a code of practice as to lay-offs in areas of federal jurisdiction in Canada and, accordingly, has initiated action in this regard with appropriate departments.
Throughout the sharp recession and prolonged and incomplete recovery in world demand, Canadian industry has sustained a higher level of output and investment than most industrialized countries. But, in the last few years it has felt the stress of rising costs of energy, materials and labour. Overhead costs have climbed because of the underutilization of capacity. In this situation some of the structural weaknesses, inherent in any changing economy, have become more obvious and more serious.
Recognizing the debilitating effects of inflation on industrial performance, the government has led the nation through a period of restraint in prices, wages, profits, and government expenditures. In preparing for the post-control period the government has confirmed its reliance on market forces and co-operation in the declaration "The Way Ahead"-1 am sure hon. members from all parties have read that closely-and elaborated these principles in "An Agenda for Co-operation". At the same time the government has set the stage for recovery and investment with its spring budget, initiating inventory allowances, and increasing investment credits and other incen-
Mining Unemployment
tives to invest, which it is to be hoped will be passed by parliament in the very near future.
Meanwhile there has been an intensive examination of the performance and potential of individual industry sectors. These are being developed in collaboration with consultative groups of businessmen and are leading to the identification of market opportunities and the potential for specialization and other avenues to increase efficiency and competitive capacity. At the same time the difficulties of adaptation to meet increasing international competition, for some products and industries, are being identified.
The examination of industry sectors has underlined the impact of the many other policies and programs of governments and private institutions on their efficiency and competitive ability. Not only specific industrial grants and incentives, but broader government policies relating to taxation, trade relations, transportation and resource development, have major effects on a wide range industrial operations. At the same time policies of both the federal and provincial governments, establishing standards for the private market place, and providing greater social equity, which I am sure the member for Nickel Belt is interested in, have a cumulative impact on the cost of business operations and investment.
In summary, the government has taken major steps to improve the environment for industrial operations and investment as international markets recover.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, having listened to the hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) I was hoping I would have as much time as he had in order to engage in meaningful debate with him and to prick some of those fanciful balloons he was flying about here this afternoon, quoting figures, always frothing at the mouth, and waxing indignant. The mere mention of certain words such as multinational just raised his hackles. Frankly, I always consider it for cosmetic effect. It sounds good, but is meaningless.
Hon. members want to know whether the mineral industry is profitable or not. It is. However, there is a fantasy about the land that Canada sits on the richest motherlodes of almost all known metals. That is the farthest from the truth. As a result of good technology, we can develop a lot of resources. However, there are dozens of places in the world that have far richer deposits of iron ore, copper, zinc, nickel, and gold, and even oil.
Alberta oil is of a type of geological formation that is among the most expensive to get at because it is pinpoint drilling. It is a matter of finding the domes in the deposits of oil and gas. It is not like in Venezuela or Saudi Arabia, drilling a deep well and finding a huge lake or very large deposit. The drilling and other costs of production in Canada are much higher. We also see this in the drilling for natural gas on the eastern slopes of the Arctic, the cost of drilling wells 16,000 and 18,000 feet. Look at the fantastic cost of drilling wells in the Arctic.
Many people, particularly the New Democrats, dismiss the cost of development of our minerals and the high risk that is involved as something they should not even know about.
I am glad that my colleague has introduced an amendment so that this motion is meaningful. If there has been unprofitable development to this day in the minerals industry in Canada, not only the exploration and development of the raw ore beds or the finding of petroleum and natural gas but the
further processing, it is because of the idiotic tax system that we had and still have.
Those of us who went through that nefarious white paper on taxation which the government produced in 1968, and saw the response from industry and from other governments, are aware that the basic premise for that so-called tax reform measure was astounding, a total misconception, fundamental ignorance of what is involved in the production and processing of minerals in this country. Fortunately, there were some changes, but not enough, and not soon enough.
When I first came to this House over 20 years ago I advocated getting rid of the so-called principal occupation rule, the rule which drove smaller investors among Canadians, as individuals or as corporate entities, out of the independent oil game. It was so much easier for our American counterparts to come in here. They had the advantage. We sat idly by and allowed the rule to stand and to drive Canadians out of the development of their own oil industry. Now the situation is different, but there is no more independent oil available; there is little or no freehold available which is likely to produce.
I have little time and I wish to turn, now, to another subject. First of all, I do not think there can be a national, unilateral mineral development strategy or industrial plan. Such a plan has to be developed with the provinces. We, as Conservatives, objected to the former minister of finance, the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Macdonald) ramming down the throat of this House his scheme for petroleum development as far as the Government of Canada was concerned. It was an outright raid on provincial jurisdiction. And if the hon. member for Nickel Belt wants to know what governments can do, let him read the judgment which was pronounced today with regard to Saskatchewan's raid on the petroleum industry and what that is going to cost those people-and the cost of $500 million was likely taken off the backs of other Canadians who were consuming Saskatchewan petroleum products. That is where the payment and the cost are involved.
